name: Projection Bias
description: People often assume other people share their own current preferences, reactions, or priorities more than they really do. In product work, this is the classic trap of designing for yourself and treating your current mental state as representative.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to personas, opportunity framing, prioritization, internal dogfooding, and UX research synthesis: designers, PMs, and researchers can project their own needs or tastes onto users and mistake self-similarity for evidence.
myth_risk_note: The label conflates two distinct literatures: behavioral economics' projection bias (predicting one's own future utility) versus social psychology's social projection (predicting others' current states). Both phenomena are real and well-documented independently, but are mechanistically different, risking design misapplication if not disambiguated.
prevalence_note: The warning against 'designing for yourself' is common in UX-research teaching and product critique, even though the exact formal label varies and is used less consistently than false consensus or curse of knowledge.

findings.description: A meta-analysis found social projection (expecting others to be similar to oneself) is substantially stronger for ingroups than outgroups, with outgroup projection positive but small. Ingroup projection is stronger for laboratory-created groups than real social categories; analysis mode and judgment order showed no discernible effects. Supports social projection functioning as an egocentric heuristic for inductive reasoning, contributing to ingroup favoritism and perceived ingroup homogeneity.
findings.source_title: Social Projection to Ingroups and Outgroups: A Review and Meta-Analysis

findings.description: Across choice and trait-judgment tasks, participants overestimated how many other people would share their own choice, belief, or behavior, and they judged dissenters as more abnormal than warranted — direct evidence for the false consensus effect as an egocentric social-perception bias.
findings.source_title: The “false consensus effect”: An egocentric bias in social perception and attribution processes

applications.title: Fat Stone Farm pivoting elderberry marketing away from an assumed winter-only season
applications.description: Fat Stone Farm, working with agency Webistry, used audience research to discover real summer demand for its elderberry products among health-conscious smoothie drinkers -- overturning an internal assumption that elderberry products were only relevant during cold/flu season.
applications.ethical_note: Using real research to correct a mistaken assumption about customer needs and serve an underserved use case (summer demand) is a genuine product-market discovery, not a persuasion technique aimed at changing behavior against a user's own interest.

applications.title: Packlane's 'Size Matters' landing page explaining packaging measurements the team assumed were obvious
applications.description: Packlane built a dedicated landing page walking customers step by step through measuring packaging dimensions and adding buffer space -- information the internal team had assumed was self-evident, until user research revealed customers didn't share that assumption.
applications.ethical_note: Correcting an internal team's mistaken assumption about what customers already know is a straightforward clarity improvement -- there's no persuasion angle, just closing a genuine information gap that was creating real customer confusion.
